# Aggivaccha Sutta (MN 72 (PTS MN i 483))

**ID:** MN 72 (PTS MN i 483)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Aggivaccha Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** With Vacchagotta on Fire
**PTS:** MN i 483
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul2.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Aggivaccha Sutta* (also known as the *Aggivacchagotta Sutta*, MN 72) records a dialogue between the Buddha and the wanderer (*paribbājaka*) Vacchagotta at the Jetavana monastery [Kuznetsova et al. 2012]. When Vacchagotta questions him regarding the ten standard unexpounded or speculative metaphysical theses (*avyākata*)—such as whether the world is eternal or finite, and whether the Tathāgata exists after death—the Buddha refuses to take any stance [Li 2012; Ozkan 2013; Rogell 2003]. The Buddha explains that entertaining such speculative dogmas leads only to distress and does not conduce to peace or enlightenment [Li 2012; Galasek 2016]. Instead, having seen the arising and cessation of the five aggregates (*khandha*), the Tathāgata is liberated through non-clinging and has relinquished all imaginings and conceits concerning a self [Sieg 2004; Koller 2016; Wen].

To elucidate the condition of a liberated mind beyond the fourfold tetralemma of existence and non-existence, the Buddha presents the famous simile of an extinguished flame [Ozkan 2013]. He asks Vacchagotta where a fire goes when its fuel of grass and wood has burned out; Vacchagotta admits that the question does not apply, as the fire is simply reckoned as extinguished for lack of sustenance [Kuznetsova et al. 2012]. Similarly, the Buddha explains that an awakened being is freed from designation by any of the five aggregates, profound and immeasurable like the great ocean, making assertions of post-mortem rebirth or non-rebirth inapplicable [Kuznetsova et al. 2012].

 Comparative scholarship highlights that while the Pāli sutta frames the unanswered questions across ten positions, the northern parallel in the Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* (T 99) expands these into the standard fourteen *avyākṛta* propositions [Li 2012].

**Sources**

- [Li 2012] Shenghai Li, Candrakīrti’s Āgama: A Study of the Concept and Uses of Scripture in Classical Indian Buddhism (2012) — Analysis of the avyākata questions, comparison of the ten Pāli alternatives with the fourteen in the Chinese Saṃyuktāgama (T 99).
- [Kuznetsova et al. 2012] Irina Kuznetsova, Jonardon Ganeri, and Chakravarthi Ram-Prasad, Hindu and Buddhist Ideas in Dialogue: Self and No-Self (2012) — Discussion of Vacchagotta as a paribbājaka interlocutor and the simile of the extinguished fire and fuel.
- [Ozkan 2013] Cuma Ozkan, Comparative Analysis: Buddhist Madhyamaka and Daoist Chongxuan (Twofold Mystery) in Early Tang (2013) — The Buddha's early use and rejection of the tetralemma regarding rebirth of an enlightened mind in MN 72.
- [Rogell 2003] Sharda Rogell, Pressing Out Pure Honey: A Practitioner’s Study Guide (Majjhima Nikāya) (2003) — Note on the ten speculative undeclared views shared between MN 72 and MN 63.
- [Sieg 2004] Petra (Tara) Sieg, Buddhism and the Earth: Environmental Thought in Early Buddhist Philosophy (2004) — The Buddha's explanation of freedom from theories and the arising and perishing of the aggregates.
- [Koller 2016] John M. Koller, The Indian Way: An Introduction to the Philosophies & Religions of India (2016) — Quotation regarding liberation from attachment, imaginings, and conceits of self.
- [Wen] Tzungkuen Wen, A Study of Sukkhavipassaka in Pali Buddhism — The Buddha's declaration of liberation through non-clinging upon contemplating the rising and falling of the five aggregates.
- [Galasek 2016] Bruno Galasek, On Presenting Characters and Representation of Persons... Characters in Narrative Suttas of the Majjhima Nikāya (2016) — Contextualization of the Buddha's refusal to enter speculative philosophical debate.
